Stated Claim / Post Context:
Todd Blanche falsely claims DOJ isn’t seeking to block Alaska from certifying Senate contest

Blanche claims DOJ's Alaska lawsuit doesn't seek to block certifying the state's election if the Republican loses. The actual complaint says otherwise.

Actual Article Body:
By Brentin Mock, Zachary Roth

October 24, 2026

to see more of our voting rights news coverage when you search.

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche claimed Saturday that the Justice Department’s lawsuit against Alaska does not seek to stop certification of the state’s U.S. Senate election results.

His own department’s complaint flatly contradicts him.

But Blanche’s attempt to reframe the lawsuit — which President Donald Trump said he personally ordered — appears to be a bid to push back against how it has been widely, and correctly, interpreted: as a dangerous effort to intrude on state authority and lay the groundwork to subvert results.

Join 350,000 readers who rely on our daily and weekly newsletters for the latest in voting, elections and democracy.

“The Department of Justice does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska’s election,” Blanche wrote on social media. “This litigation seeks to ensure that after Alaskans cast their ballots, they are preserved in a manner so that only Alaska’s governing officials have the information necessary to make a determination as to whether Alaskan voters were confused or mislead.”

The lawsuit was spurred by the inclusion of a candidate on the ballot with the name Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. That’s similar to the name of theincumbent, Sen. Daniel Sullivan (R), who is running for reelection.

DOJ claims in its lawsuit that voters will be confused by the similar names.

“Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan,” the complaint alleges, “the State and its officers will fail in its (sic) obligation to protect the integrity of its election.”

It continues:

‘[I]t is vital that Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion. An election result may be impacted by voter confusion if: (1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska’s rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election.”

DOJ then asks the court to “[d]eclare that certification of any result that may be impacted by voter confusion, as defined above, would violate Defendants’ duties under the NVRA to ‘protect the integrity of the electoral process.’”

It also asks the court to block the state “from certifying any result that may be impacted by voter confusion, as defined above, pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan and any further procedures or relief this Court deems necessary and appropriate to determine what the result would have been absent Daniel J. Sullivan’s inclusion on the ballot.”

(DOJ appears to leave out a key verb at the start of the sentence above, but in context the meaning is clear.)

Those are the only steps DOJ asks the court to take, other than to “award any other relief it deems just and proper.” Despite what Blanche claims, the lawsuit says nothing about requiring election officials to preserve ballots, which in any case would do little to reveal whether voters were confused.

In other words, DOJ asks the court to stop the certification of Alaska’s Senate election until an investigation into the role played by voter confusion can be conducted. The “investigation” would entail giving all of the votes for Daniel J. Sullivan to the incumbent.

And as former Obama administration official and TIME magazine editor Richard Stengel points out, the lawsuit says nothing about the voters who might mistakenly think they are voting for the challenger Sullivan but instead vote for Sen. Sullivan.

It’s inarguable that the lawsuit does aim to stop certification, even if temporarily, in order to try to change the result.

More importantly, Blanche’s effort to instead present the lawsuit as a modest attempt to guard against the effect of voter confusion suggests the DOJ may have overplayed its hand. And that it now sees a need to fight off the idea that the lawsuit aims to challenge results and potentially subvert a GOP loss.

Jack Dorsey’s Block released a new voice model out of the company’s research lab that runs locally and sounds strangely human with its expressions like laughs, pauses, and cries. The company said the model, called Dessa, is trained fully on human speech and a single NVIDIA GPU rack.

Dessa is a full-duplex model, which means it can talk and listen at the same time, just like the GPT-Live model OpenAI released earlier this year. Typically, speech models are paired with a large language model for knowledge retrieval. Block said that Dessa’s knowledge stems from the conversational data it has.

We believe voice is the most natural way to interact with intelligence, so we created Dessa, the most authentic full-duplex speech model ever built. Talking with it feels like talking with a person…full of emotion, nuance, pauses, and a natural cadence. https://t.co/r0qFLdvd6c

Block said that the current models can sound unnatural and annoying because they have text in the pipeline that drives speech generation. A lot of models like ElevenLabs v4 or Fish Audio Drama 3 use voice tags to drive emotion in speech generation. Dorsey’s company claims that emotion is built into its model. It’s not clear if that emotion is being steered by some kind of tags.

“Interacting with current voice AI can just plain suck. It turns your voice into text and throws away an incredible amount of information text alone can’t carry. The most powerful AIs in the world can’t hear how you feel. We think that’s ridiculous, leads to a worse experience, and is potentially dangerous,” the company said in a blog post.

The company’s researchers posted multiple examples of conversations with Dessa where the agent had different voices, cadences, and emotions. For instance, in the conversation, the bot said it was tired from work, and at that point it sounded tired.

We made the first AI model you can have a realistic conversation with that was trained entirely on speech!Dessa is a full-duplex speech-to-speech model that you can run on consumer GPUs.This is a GPT3 moment for speech. pic.twitter.com/XVD8sSyJn8

In the example below, the bot was talking about the person making it comfortable while sounding emotional and almost breaking down.

Dessa=full-duplex speech model vs Human=me, https://t.co/1eI6QFHo1w pic.twitter.com/zlZfxH2BA5

Another one shows a Block team member playing a game with the voice assistant.

For the love of the game.Watch Cara play a guessing game with Dessa. The model guesses the first one right straight away, and the second doesn’t take long either.https://t.co/FDmoXNPpIh pic.twitter.com/I9f8saduEA

The company said that the model can run locally on a consumer-grade computer such as a MacBook M4 Max or better. However, there is no public access to Dessa at the moment, and Block has put out a call for safety researchers to test the model. This is likely to test out cases where a voice agent could trick people on the other end.

Block is in the business of finance and selling its solutions to small businesses. Square already uses voice AI to handle ordering. But with its own voice model that can run on-device, it can power a lot more business and consumer experiences at a lower cost.

Orphaned Alaska walrus calf makes 4,000-mile journey to new home at SeaWorld Orlando

Annautaq, an orphaned 5-month-old walrus calf rescued from an Alaskan beach, has found a new home at SeaWorld Orlando.

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

An orphaned baby walrus from Alaska recently found a new home over 4,000 miles away at Florida’s SeaWorld.

US Geological Survey biologist Tony Fischbach and intern Violet Anniskett found the 5-month-old, 220-pound walrus calf on a beach in Point Lay in Northern Alaska on Sept. 14, according to the Alaska Sealife Center.

The researchers were scouring the remote beach after a walrus herd left during heavy surf.

They were collecting carcass samples to study algal toxins.

The lone mammal, who they named Annautaq, was found lying on the sand between two dead walruses.

Fischbach and Anniskett immediately jumped into action to save Annautaq, and moved him more than half a mile to an abandoned building where he could be safe from predators until more help could arrive.

“When we found him, a determined flock of gulls was intent on scavenging him. He was in immediate peril of suffering this fate had we not gotten approval to intervene. Two polar bears were also active on the island,” Fischbach said.

The heroic pair stayed there with the calf for three days until a transport team for the walrus finally arrived.

Annautaq, which means “axe” in Iñupiaq, was then flown to the Alaska Sealife Center more than 800 miles away in Seward to start his recovery.

Veterinarians said he was in decent condition, but he was dehydrated and was covered in wounds.

And he was lonely.

Baby walruses need constant care from their moms when they are young. Without that connection, he had actually quickly bonded with Fischbach and Anniskett during the days they stayed with him.

“He bonded with us fast and wouldn’t sleep unless one of us was in the room. It was just us two for three days, stuck in a storm with the young walrus,” Anniskett said.

While he was recovering well, the US Fish and Wildlife Service ruled that the walrus couldn’t be released back into the wild.

Experts decided the best place for him would be SeaWorld in Orlando, where he was transported this month, SeaWorld said on Oct. 21.

The marine mammal park has a “longstanding rescue mission” that has already helped more than 43,000 animals in need, SeaWorld said.

He’ll be quarantined for 30 days and will receive 24-hour support, including six bottle feedings every day.

“At this young age, Annautaq needs more than nutrition and veterinary care. He also needs close contact and companionship, which our expert team is providing around the clock,” said Jim Kinsler, a curator at SeaWorld Orlando.

“As he settles in, we’ll make introductions to [other walruses] Garfield, Kaboodle and Uki at his pace. Kaboodle’s experience caring for rescued calves and the opportunity to connect with two-year old Uki, herself a rescued walrus, make this herd a promising setting for him to learn, build relationships and grow.”

Kaboodle’s experience caring for rescued calves and the opportunity to connect with two-year old Uki, herself a rescued walrus, make this herd a promising setting for him to learn, build relationships and grow.”
